cells.tense: The hours are returning what you put into them, and the room is yours.
cells.act: stand in the gap it leaves without rebuilding yet
cells.ask: Do the daily thing as usual, then sit where the work stopped and don't fill the space. Notice what wants to go back in, and hold off a while.
cells.core:
What you've built with repetition is holding. The practice has your attention in it, not your worry — that's the difference between sharpening something and guarding it. You can be alone with the work a while and come back to people more yourself, not less.

There's a stretch where the habit runs itself and the next thing isn't obvious. That isn't the practice failing; it's the practice having done its job on the old form. The act here is to stand in the gap it leaves without rebuilding yet. So the ask is smaller than it sounds — do the thing once more, then sit in the open minute after it and don't reach for the next move. The gap is where the useful next thing will come from, and it won't if you mortar it over tonight.
cells.sheetLine: The practice holds. Leave one gap unbuilt.
cells.verb: keeping a small flame lit by attention
cells.place: where the architecture gets drawn before anyone builds

cells.tense: The next repetition is already being rehearsed, and stopping is the thing you're bracing against.
cells.act: surrender the outcome and keep the act
cells.ask: Find the piece you keep reopening. Take it once to where anyone reasonable would say done, then keep showing up — only not again on that piece.
cells.core:
The refining has gotten past the making. Solitude that used to feed you has started to feel like the only safe place to stand, and underneath is a question you haven't asked: what happens if it goes unfinished. Nothing does. That's the fear talking, not the fact.

The act that fits is to surrender the outcome and keep the act. You still show up, you still do the thing — only the ending stops being yours to decide. The small form: choose the piece you keep reopening, take it to where any reasonable person would say done, and stop there. Not the whole practice — that piece. The grip you release is on the finish, not on the hours.
cells.sheetLine: Still show up. Stop deciding when it's finished.
cells.verb: keeping a small flame lit by attention

cells.tense: The practice has been set down, and the reasons it can't be taken up again live further back than the present.
cells.act: give back what is owed, and take what is yours
cells.ask: Something you used to do regularly could come back this week — a short block, twenty minutes is plenty — and then you stop. Nothing bigger is being asked.
cells.core:
There's a version of this where the hours came easily and a version where they stopped, and the second is where you're standing. The practice isn't lost — it's sitting on the far side of something that made trying feel like too much. What's missing now isn't will. It's a fair exchange: you were putting in more than came back, so you stopped putting in.

A small act of giving back what is owed and taking what is yours fits here. Not a new regimen. Something you used to do, one short block this week, taken without asking whether it's enough. Twenty minutes is a fair trade for a day. When it's over, stop — don't measure it against the old hours. The measure is that it happened.
cells.sheetLine: One short block this week, then stop measuring it.

cells.tense: The skill is arriving in the room while your account of how it got there says you never practiced.
cells.act: dream it from what you have already lived
cells.ask: Say or put on a page how you actually got good at this, as plainly as you can. Then one line about what else is worth building from here.
cells.core:
People bring you problems in this area and you solve them, and when asked how, you say it's nothing — luck, a knack that came with you. The hours are there; the story that says you didn't sit with them is doing those hours a disservice. What looks like talent is a long practice that got filed under something else.

The act that fits is to dream it from what you have already lived. Not a new plan — a truer account of the old one. This week, say or put on a page how you actually got good at the thing you call natural, then a line about what you'd build next if the skill were clearly yours and not an accident. The account is the author showing up. The line is what the account is for.
cells.sheetLine: Say how you got good. Then say what's next.
cells.verb: keeping a small flame lit by attention
cells.place: where the architecture gets drawn before anyone builds
